newsitem.title: USA: Lighter, sexy Batman flies back to movie theaters.
newsitem.headline: Lighter, sexy Batman flies back to movie theaters.

text.p: Can George Clooney, star of the hit TV show "E.R.," save Batman from drowning in his own dark past? Will sexy Alicia Silverstone and muscleman Arnold Schwarzenegger wield a powerful one-two box office punch?

Stay tuned, Batfans! The answer is coming on Friday to a theatre certain to be near your home. "Batman and Robin," fourth in a series of movies based on the nearly 60-year-old comic book character, arrives with a new pair of villains and anxious fans waiting to see what its stars and director, Joel Schumacher, have cooked up.

"We've had almost 60 years of the 'woe is me,' angst-ridden, self-obsessed Batman. I didn't want that for this audience," Schumacher told Reuters. "What George has added to the Batman franchise is humanity."
In the first three movies, the Caped Crusader brooded over the death of his parents when he was a boy and lamented over his sometimes lonely double life as millionaire Bruce Wayne.

The first two, "Batman" in 1989 and "Batman Returns" in 1992, featured Michael Keaton as the crime-fighting superhero and garnered over $410 million in U.S. ticket sales for Warner Bros. studios, the film's distributor. The third, "Batman Forever" (1995), put Val Kilmer behind Batman's dark mask and scored one of the biggest opening weekends ever with $52.7 million and grossed $184 million.

Combined, the movies have become a franchise for Warner Bros., making the new film's success an important milestone for the studio. With this summer's long list of action-packed movies costing well over $100 million, Schumacher felt he had to make the Batman sequel stand out from the pack.
At home, Bruce Wayne sheds the fatherly wing of long-time butler Alfred and begins shepherding the lives of sidekick Robin, played by Chris O'Donnell, and Batgirl (Silverstone).

Don't be confused, though, by the warmer, compassionate superhero. "Batman and Robin" contains all the outlandish action fans want, along with evil plots to destroy the world and larger-than-life villains like "Mr. Freeze" played by Schwarzenegger and "Poison Ivy" portrayed by Uma Thurman.

Gotham City is under the icy threat of Mr. Freeze, who wants to chill the city to its steely bone, then grab its precious diamonds. He's helped by the oversexed Ivy, who wants to save the world's plants from pollution.
Noble goal, Ivy's, but poor execution. Though she is nearly able to split the dynamic duo using her sex appeal, Ivy is foiled by Batgirl, who also has caught Robin's eye.

But this Batgirl is not all about sex appeal. Silverstone, who rocketed to fame as heroine of "Clueless," is a street-smart computer whiz who races motorcycles but is still sweet enough to tuck Albert, her uncle, into bed at night.

"It's great for girls to see a young woman as strong and smart as the guys," said Schumacher, adding that he was determined to avoid making this "Batman" into a retread. "And for the guys, they can see Alicia Silverstone in a black rubber suit being sexy."
